title: How to run a club shoot
summary: How to organise a small Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting club shoot step by step: venue, format, layouts, people, safety and results, with your volunteers planned in.

body.html: A club shoot is a good way to bring people together and give beginners a first taste of competition. A club, a shooting ground or a group of shooters can organise one. Start with the basics: agree the date and terms with the ground owner. Then find out which permits, insurance and safety rules apply in your country.

Next, decide the format: Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting, the number of targets, the categories (who competes against whom, for example by age) and the entry fee. You can use the FITASC rules as a basis. Announce in advance which rules you will shoot under, and any local changes.

html.sporting: The course designers (the people who decide where each target flies) show the layouts and targets to the jury members in charge and to the chief referee. Those officials can ask for changes for safety, for easier refereeing or to protect nature before they approve the layouts.
html.compak: The layouts are set before the start, with the person in charge of the ground present. FITASC technical committee members, or the jury if none is there, check that the trajectories are safe, varied and balanced.

body.html: For a club event, follow the same idea on a small scale. Ask an experienced referee to look at the trajectories before the start, with safety first.

html.sporting: Before the event nobody may practise on the competition layouts, not even the organisers.
html.compak: Shooters may practise on the competition trajectories, but with the targets combined differently. The setting table (the written plan of which traps are shot from each station) used for practice must differ from the competition one.

body.html: At a club shoot you set your own practice rule. Write it in the programme so that everyone has the same chance.
Look after the people: referees, trappers, registration and scoring. Make up the squads (who shoots with whom) and a timetable, and publish both in advance.

Under FITASC rules, everyone near the shooting wears hearing protection, spectators included. Shooters, referees and staff also wear safety glasses; in Sporting™, so does anyone close to a stand. At a club shoot, many organisers simply ask everyone to wear both.

End the day with the prize giving and a thank-you to all helpers. Then publish the results: tidy score sheets and a clear results table show respect for the participants. If you want the results on ClayArena, contact ClayArena and ask in what form to send them.

Plan your volunteers early. They can register shooters, help with scoring under the referee's eye, look after parking, take photos and clear up cases and target fragments. Give a safety briefing to anyone who will work near a trap. The helper's side of the story: Club life and volunteering.

key_points.html: Start by agreeing terms with the ground and checking local rules, permits and insurance.
Announce the format, the rules and the practice rule in advance.
Ask an experienced referee to check the trajectories before the start.
Ask everyone near the shooting to wear hearing protection and glasses.
Plan referees, trappers, registration, results and volunteers, with a safety briefing.

did_you_know.html: Under the Sporting™ rules, squad lists and start times for international events are published in advance. Doing the same at a club shoot saves many questions on the day.

quiz.q: Where do you start when organising a club shoot?

options.text: By agreeing terms with the ground

quiz.explain: First come the venue, the terms, the permits and safety.

quiz.q: Who designs the layouts of an international Sporting™ competition?
quiz.explain: In Sporting™ the course designer prepares the layouts, and officials check them before the start. In Compak® Sporting the jury can instead pick ready-made setting tables.

quiz.q: Where may shooters practise on the competition trajectories before the event?

options.text: In Sporting™, on the competition layouts
In Compak® Sporting, with the targets combined differently

quiz.explain: In Sporting™ nobody may practise on the competition layouts. In Compak® Sporting practice is allowed, but with a different setting table, so the targets are combined differently.
